newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Lufthansa to fight fare ruling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lufthansa to fight fare ruling.

text.p: German airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG said on Wednesday it would fight a ruling by the Federal Cartel Office that its Frankfurt-Berlin fares were too high, arguing its domestic routes were in fact unprofitable.

The cartel office, Germany's main competition authority, had earlier issued an official warning to the airline that its Frankfurt-Berlin fares were excessive and demanded that the airline make a response within a month.
Lufthansa immediately rejected both the criticism of its pricing contained in the cartel office's statement and the warning itself.

"The warning itself has no legal effect of its own and comprises a number of legally-disputed questions," the airline said in a statement. It added it would seek a full legal clarification of the implications as soon as possible.

Lufthansa, which charges 840 marks ($525.7) for its return Frankfurt-Berlin Business Class fare, said such a fare could not represent an abuse of its dominant market position because it failed to cover its costs on the route.
"Companies cannot be forced to set prices, which make break-even or profit-yielding production possible," it said.
It added: "The fact that another competitor has for years flown along its domestic German routes at a loss underlines that the routes cannot be served in a commercially-viable way".

Deutsche BA, an airline 49 percent-owned by British Airways Plc, flies seven German domestic routes and earlier this month revamped its fare structure in a way which reduces the price distinction between economy and business fares.
Deutsche BA's fare structure will from January 20 include "super-value" fares of 190 marks for its domestic routes, rising to a "flexi-ticket" with full re-booking options that will cost 520 marks.
A spokeswoman for the airline said it had no comment to make on the cartel office warning.

Lufthansa's rejection of the cartel office's warning could now mean the matter has to go before Berlin's Court of Appeals court, the competent body to decide appeals made against cartel office rulings.
If a full appeal is lodged, a final decision could take as long as a year to emerge.
